listen.explanationKey: What does the Bill of Rights protect?
facts: The Constitution was written in 1787. Many Americans wanted it to say clearly which rights the government can never take away.
So in 1791, ten amendments were added to the Constitution. These first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights.
It protects the basic rights of Americans and of people living in the United States.
Freedom of speech and freedom of religion are two of these rights.

newWords.meaning: the first ten amendments to the Constitution
the right to say what you think
the amendment that protects freedom of speech, religion, the press, assembly and petition

story.say: The Constitution was written in 1787.

help.simpler: The Constitution was written in the year 1787.
help.example: That was four years after the war with Britain ended.
help.why: Knowing this date helps you understand why the Bill of Rights came later.

story.say: Many Americans wanted it to say clearly which rights the government can never take away.

help.simpler: Many people wanted the Constitution to list the rights the government must always respect.
help.example: They wanted it to say clearly that people can speak freely and choose their own religion.
help.why: This is why the Bill of Rights was added.

story.say: So in 1791, ten amendments were added to the Constitution.

help.simpler: In 1791, ten changes were added to the Constitution.
help.example: These ten amendments were added together, four years after the Constitution was written.
help.why: These first ten amendments have a special name: the Bill of Rights.

story.say: These first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights.

help.simpler: The first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights.
help.example: Today you can see the Bill of Rights at the National Archives in Washington, D.C.
help.why: The Bill of Rights is one of the most important parts of the Constitution.

story.say: It protects the basic rights of Americans and of people living in the United States.

help.simpler: The Bill of Rights keeps the basic rights of everyone in the country safe.
help.example: It protects people who live in the United States, not only citizens.
help.why: The test asks what the Bill of Rights protects: the basic rights of Americans and of people living here.

story.say: Freedom of speech and freedom of religion are two of these rights.

help.simpler: You can say what you think, and you can practice any religion, or no religion.
help.example: You can disagree with the government in public without being punished for it.

lessons.title: No one is above the law

listen.explanationKey: What is the rule of law?
facts: The rule of law means everyone must follow the law. Leaders and the government must obey the law too.
No one is above the law. For example, the President must pay taxes like everyone else. A mayor who steals can be arrested and go to court like anyone else.
The government has three branches so one part does not become too powerful. Each branch can check the others. This is called checks and balances.
For example, Congress writes laws, the President can veto them, and the courts can decide a law goes against the Constitution.

newWords.meaning: each branch can limit the power of the others
the power of government is split into parts

story.say: The rule of law means everyone must follow the law.

help.simpler: Everyone has to follow the law.
help.example: Drivers must stop at a red light, whether they are rich or poor, famous or not.
help.why: The test asks: What is the rule of law? “Everyone must follow the law” is one answer.

story.say: Leaders and the government must obey the law too. No one is above the law.

help.simpler: Even leaders and the government must follow the law. No one is special.
help.example: If a leader breaks the law, they can be taken to court too.
help.why: “Leaders must obey the law” and “No one is above the law” are also correct answers.

check.statement: Leaders do not have to obey the law.

story.say: For example, the President must pay taxes like everyone else.

help.simpler: The President pays taxes, just like you.
help.example: The President follows the same tax laws as everyone else.
help.why: This example shows that the rule of law applies to everyone, even the highest leader.

story.say: A mayor who steals can be arrested and go to court like anyone else.

help.simpler: If a mayor steals, police can arrest the mayor, like anyone else.
help.example: A judge decides the case, using the same laws used for everyone.
help.why: This example shows that leaders are not above the law.

story.say: The government has three branches so one part does not become too powerful.

help.simpler: The government is split into three parts so no one part has all the power.
help.example: Congress makes laws, the President carries out laws, and the courts explain laws.
help.why: The test asks why there are three branches. “So one part does not become too powerful” is one answer.

check.prompt: Why are there three branches of government?
choices: So one part does not become too powerful
So the President can make every law

story.say: Each branch can check the others. This is called checks and balances.

help.simpler: Each part of the government can stop or limit the other parts.
help.example: It is like a team where each player watches the others to keep the game fair.
help.why: “Checks and balances” is another answer to why there are three branches.

story.say: Congress writes laws, the President can veto them, and the courts can decide a law goes against the Constitution.

help.simpler: Each branch has a way to stop the others from doing too much.
help.example: If Congress passes a law the President does not like, the President can say no. That is a veto.
help.why: These examples show checks and balances at work.

listen.explanationKey: What is the form of government of the United States?
facts: The United States is a republic: the people vote for leaders, and those leaders make laws for them.
This is also called a representative democracy. “Representative” means the leaders speak and act for the people who elected them.
It is also a constitution-based federal republic: the Constitution is the highest law, and power is shared between the national government and the states.
The economic system of the United States is capitalism, also called a free market economy. People and businesses can own things and decide what to make, buy and sell.
Think of a supermarket: stores choose what to sell and what price to ask, and you choose what to buy. Most of the time, the government does not decide this for you. That is a free market.

newWords.meaning: a country where the people elect their leaders
an economy where people and businesses own and run things
when people and businesses, not the government, decide what to make, sell and buy

story.say: The United States is a republic: the people vote for leaders, and those leaders make laws for them.

help.simpler: In the United States, people choose leaders, and the leaders make the laws.
help.example: You vote for a member of Congress. That person votes on laws for you.
help.why: The test asks about the form of government. “Republic” is one answer.

story.say: This is also called a representative democracy.

help.simpler: This is another name for the same idea: people choose leaders to represent them.
help.example: A representative speaks for the people in their area.
help.why: “Representative democracy” is another correct answer.

check.prompt: What is the form of government of the United States?

story.say: “Representative” means the leaders speak and act for the people who elected them.

help.simpler: Leaders work for the people who voted for them.
help.example: If many people in your area want a new law, your representative can speak for them in Congress.
help.why: This explains what the word “representative” means.

check.prompt: In a republic, who makes the laws? Tap them.

story.say: It is also a constitution-based federal republic.

help.simpler: This is a long name. It means the Constitution is the top law, and power is shared.
help.example: Constitution-based: built on the Constitution. Federal: power is shared with the states.
help.why: “Constitution-based federal republic” is the third correct answer about the form of government.

story.say: The Constitution is the highest law, and power is shared between the national government and the states.

help.simpler: The national government and the states each have their own powers.
help.example: The national government prints money. States give out driver’s licenses.
help.why: Sharing power keeps any one government from becoming too strong.

story.say: The economic system of the United States is capitalism, also called a free market economy.

help.simpler: The U.S. economy is capitalism. Another name is a free market economy.
help.example: Most businesses are owned by people, not by the government.
help.why: The test asks about the economic system. “Capitalism” and “free market economy” are both correct.

check.prompt: What is the economic system of the United States?

story.say: People and businesses can own things and decide what to make, buy and sell.

help.simpler: People can own homes and businesses, and choose what to make, buy and sell.
help.example: Someone can open a restaurant and decide what food to sell.
help.why: Owning things and choosing freely are at the heart of a free market.

story.say: Think of a supermarket: stores choose what to sell and what price to ask, and you choose what to buy.

help.simpler: Stores choose what they sell and the price. You choose what to buy.
help.example: If one store asks too much for apples, you can buy them at another store.
help.why: This everyday example shows how a free market works.

story.say: Most of the time, the government does not decide this for you. That is a free market.

help.simpler: Most of the time, buyers and sellers decide, not the government.
help.example: The government still makes some rules, like food safety rules, but it does not run the stores.
help.why: This is what a free market economy means, one answer on the test.
